Modeling Guilty Minds, Study 2: NLP, Random Forest & SHAP Analysis¶

The Study 1 machine learning analyses, repeated on Study 2 (not registered)¶

David George Kamper, Andrew Bistras, Jaime Castrellon¶

This notebook repeats on Study 2 the analyses of the Study 1 notebook (MPC_NLP_SHAP_Analysis_2.0.ipynb), with the same code and the same settings. It fits random forest classifiers that predict the category each participant chose from the six vignette features, with and without the belief rating; computes SHAP feature importance, overall and for each category; embeds the 64 vignettes with BGE-large (primary) and MiniLM (a check); projects them with UMAP; runs the representational similarity analysis (RSA); and analyzes the free-text justifications with embeddings, BERTopic topics and a classifier that predicts the choice from the justification. The seed, models, hyperparameters, cross-validation folds and figure style are the ones Study 1 used.

None of these analyses is in the Study 2 preregistration. They are exploratory, and the manuscript should describe them as unregistered analyses that repeat the Study 1 machine learning analyses. The registered analyses are in MPC_Study2_Analysis.Rmd; this notebook runs after it and changes nothing in it.

The same code also runs on the Study 1 data in the folder, and the first thing to check is that it reproduces the published Study 1 numbers. When it does, any difference between the studies comes from the data and not from the code. Two questions matter most for the revision: whether the Study 1 SHAP pattern for Knowledge, in which the contents of the package mattered more than the payment, appears again in Study 2, and whether the RSA result replicates.

Several additions go beyond the Study 1 notebook, and each is labeled where it appears. The most important uses Study 2's three probe questions, which define a second category for every case: Knowledge if the participant answered that he knew, or was practically certain, that illicit material was in the package; otherwise Recklessness if he was aware of a substantial risk of it; otherwise Negligence if he should have been aware of that risk; otherwise Blamelessness. The random forest, SHAP, RSA, topic and text analyses are repeated with this probe-defined category as the outcome. The other additions check the Study 1 results themselves: a participant bootstrap shows how stable the SHAP ranking of the features is, a table of plain percentages gives the direction that SHAP importances leave out, a permutation p value for the RSA treats the 64 vignettes rather than the 2,016 vignette pairs as the units, the vignette means of the two studies are correlated directly, the text classifier is rerun with balanced class weights, and the topics are crossed with the registered justification codes. A closing table sets each published Study 1 number beside its rerun and its Study 2 counterparts.

In both studies the slider asked what the defendant believed was the chance that illicit material was in the package, so this notebook calls it the belief rating; the Study 1 notebook called it the risk slider. The category chosen from the four Model Penal Code options is called the choice. Figures are saved as PDFs without titles in output/nlp/figures, with the prefix fig_s2_ (grayscale, except the SHAP beeswarm and dependence plots, which keep SHAP's colors as in Study 1), and tables are saved as CSV files in output/nlp for the combined report. The notebook never prints an individual justification.

0. Environment Setup¶

In Colab, open this notebook from the study2_analysis folder in Google Drive, choose a GPU runtime if one is available (Runtime, then Change runtime type, then T4 GPU), and set FOLDER_IN_DRIVE below to the folder's location in Drive. The notebook reads only data/processed/study2_trials.csv, data/study1_trials.csv and materials/mensReaVignettes_binary.json, and data/processed/justification_codes.csv for one optional table, so the raw Pavlovia files and the Prolific export can stay off Drive. In a local Jupyter session, start Jupyter from the study2_analysis folder. A full run takes about twenty-five minutes on a machine with two processor cores, almost half of it the bootstrap in Section 6; a GPU shortens the embedding steps in Sections 3 and 9.

1. Data Loading & Preprocessing¶

Study 2 comes from data/processed/study2_trials.csv, written by 01b_assemble_tables.R: one row per case, five cases per person, for everyone in the full sample (all completers who passed the registered exclusions), which is the primary sample of the registered analysis. Setting SAMPLE = "first_200" in the setup cell restricts the analyses to the first 200 completions and writes the outputs to a separate folder. The six features are coded 1 for the level the Study 1 notebook treated as more incriminating: a biker rather than an uncle, a duffel bag rather than a gift-wrapped package, being told what was inside rather than asking, $1,000 rather than no payment, Mexico rather than Canada, and fentanyl rather than drugs for a rare disease.

Study 1 comes from data/study1_trials.csv, the file the Study 1 notebook read. Its exclusion (participants with exactly five trials) and its feature coding are applied exactly as in that notebook, and its row order is kept, so its cross-validation folds are the same ones.

In both studies the culpability score runs from 1 (Blamelessness) to 4 (Knowledge), and every case's six features are checked against the text of the vignette it showed. The probe-defined category (Study 2 only) follows the registered analysis: Knowledge if the answer to the KNEW question was Yes; otherwise Recklessness if the answer to AWARE was Yes; otherwise Negligence if the answer to SHOULD was Yes; otherwise Blamelessness.

In [4]:
# ── Categories and features (the Study 1 definitions) ──
JUDGMENT_ORDER = ['Blamelessness', 'Negligence', 'Recklessness', 'Knowledge']
culp_map = {'Blamelessness': 1, 'Negligence': 2, 'Recklessness': 3, 'Knowledge': 4}

FEATURES = ['source', 'package', 'inquiry', 'payment', 'location', 'contents']
FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER = [f + '_bin' for f in FEATURES]
FEATURE_COLS = ['belief'] + FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER          # the belief rating first, as in the Study 1 notebook
FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER = ['Source (biker)', 'Package (duffel)', 'Inquiry (told)',
                            'Payment ($1000)', 'Location (Mexico)', 'Contents (fentanyl)']
FEATURE_LABELS = ['Belief rating'] + FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER

# ── Study 2 ──
s2 = pd.read_csv("data/processed/study2_trials.csv", dtype={"vignette_id": str, "participant": str})
if SAMPLE == "first_200":
    s2 = s2[s2["first_200"].astype(str).str.upper() == "TRUE"]
d2 = pd.DataFrame({
    "pid": s2["participant"].values,
    "position": s2["vignette_position"].astype(int).values,
    "vignette_id": s2["vignette_id"].str.zfill(6).values,
    "judgment": s2["choice"].values,
    "belief": s2["slider"].astype(float).values,
    "justification": s2["justification"].values,
    "knew": s2["knew"].values, "aware": s2["aware"].values, "should": s2["should"].values})
for f in FEATURES:
    d2[f + "_bin"] = s2[f].astype(int).values
d2["probe_judgment"] = np.select(
    [d2["knew"].values == "Yes", d2["aware"].values == "Yes", d2["should"].values == "Yes"],
    ["Knowledge", "Recklessness", "Negligence"], default="Blamelessness")

# ── Study 1, with the Study 1 notebook's exclusion and coding ──
raw1 = pd.read_csv("data/study1_trials.csv", dtype={"vignette_id": str})
completions = raw1.groupby("session_id").size()
r1 = raw1[raw1["session_id"].isin(completions.index[completions == 5])]
d1 = pd.DataFrame({
    "pid": r1["session_id"].values,
    "position": r1["vignette_position"].astype(int).values,
    "vignette_id": r1["vignette_id"].astype(str).str.zfill(6).values,
    "judgment": r1["judgment"].values,
    "belief": r1["slider_value"].astype(float).values,
    "justification": r1["justification"].values})
d1["source_bin"]   = (r1["source"].values == "biker").astype(int)
d1["package_bin"]  = (r1["package"].values == "duffel_bag").astype(int)
d1["inquiry_bin"]  = (r1["inquiry"].values == "source_tells").astype(int)
d1["payment_bin"]  = (r1["payment"].str.replace(",", "").str.strip().values == "$1000").astype(int)
d1["location_bin"] = (r1["location"].values == "Mexico").astype(int)
d1["contents_bin"] = (r1["contents"].values == "fentanyl").astype(int)

for d in (d1, d2):
    d["culpability"] = d["judgment"].map(culp_map)
d2["probe_culpability"] = d2["probe_judgment"].map(culp_map)

# ── Check every case's features against the text of its vignette ──
with open("materials/mensReaVignettes_binary.json", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    vignette_json = json.load(fh)
templates = {v["id"].zfill(6): v["vignette"] for v in vignette_json}

def text_features(t):
    return [int("biker" in t), int("duffel" in t), int(" tells " in t),
            int("$1000" in t), int("[MEXICO_LOC]" in t), int("fentanyl" in t)]

STUDIES = {"Study 1": d1, "Study 2": d2}
for name, d in STUDIES.items():

    assert (from_text == d[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values).all(), f"{name}: features disagree with the vignette text"
    assert d["culpability"].notna().all() and d.groupby("pid").size().eq(5).all()

          "every case's six features match its vignette text.")

print()
print("Judgment distribution:")

                    "Study 2 choice": d2["judgment"].value_counts(),
                    "Study 2 probe-defined": d2["probe_judgment"].value_counts()}).reindex(JUDGMENT_ORDER))

2. Vignette Text Reconstruction¶

As in the Study 1 notebook, each vignette's text comes from the experiment's JSON file (mensReaVignettes_binary.json), with the three placeholders replaced by fixed constants ("John", "Winnipeg, Canada" and "Nogales, Mexico"), because the name and town were randomized on each trial and are not part of the manipulation. Embedding distances therefore reflect only the six manipulated features.

Both studies used the same 64 vignettes from the same file, so the vignette texts and their embeddings are identical for the two studies and only the judgments differ. The vignette ID (six digits, read left to right as source, package, inquiry, payment, location and contents) serves as the key for each vignette; the Study 1 notebook used a string of the six feature levels, which identifies the same 64 vignettes.

In [5]:
# ── Build vignette texts from the ground-truth JSON ──
def fill_template(template):
    # Replace the JSON placeholders with fixed constants (as in the Study 1 notebook).
    return (template
            .replace('[NAME]', 'John')
            .replace('[CANADA_LOC]', 'Winnipeg, Canada')
            .replace('[MEXICO_LOC]', 'Nogales, Mexico'))

json_text_lookup = {vid: fill_template(t) for vid, t in templates.items()}
VIGNETTE_IDS = sorted(json_text_lookup)          # the 64 vignettes, in ID order
for name, d in STUDIES.items():
    d["vignette_text"] = d["vignette_id"].map(json_text_lookup)
    assert d["vignette_text"].notna().all()
    print(f"{name}: all {len(d)} trials matched to their vignette text; {d['vignette_id'].nunique()} different vignettes shown.")
print(f"JSON lookup built: {len(VIGNETTE_IDS)} vignettes")

Study 2: all 1310 trials matched to their vignette text; 64 different vignettes shown.

3. Sentence-Transformer Embeddings¶

We embed the unique vignette texts using two models, as in Study 1. The primary model is BAAI/bge-large-en-v1.5 (1024 dimensions), which pools through the CLS token and was trained contrastively with hard negatives, so it is built to tell similar texts apart; this matters because the vignettes share most of their wording. The check is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (384 dimensions, mean pooling), a widely used lightweight model that shows whether the RSA depends on the choice of embedding model. Both are pinned to the repository versions the Study 1 notebook used. The justification embeddings are computed in Section 9.

In [6]:
# ── Load embedding models ──
st_model_bge = SentenceTransformer(BGE_MODEL, revision=BGE_REVISION)
st_model_mini = SentenceTransformer(MINI_MODEL, revision=MINI_REVISION)
print("Embedding device:", st_model_bge.device)

# ── Embed the 64 vignette texts with both models ──
unique_texts = [json_text_lookup[v] for v in VIGNETTE_IDS]
vignette_embeddings_bge = st_model_bge.encode(unique_texts, batch_size=32, normalize_embeddings=True)
vignette_embeddings_mini = st_model_mini.encode(unique_texts, batch_size=32, normalize_embeddings=True)
key_to_embedding_bge = dict(zip(VIGNETTE_IDS, vignette_embeddings_bge))
key_to_embedding_mini = dict(zip(VIGNETTE_IDS, vignette_embeddings_mini))

print(f"BGE embedding shape: {vignette_embeddings_bge.shape}")
print(f"MiniLM embedding shape: {vignette_embeddings_mini.shape}")

4. UMAP Dimensionality Reduction¶

As in Study 1, UMAP projects the 64 vignette embeddings (BGE-large) into two dimensions, with the Study 1 settings, and the projection is colored by the vignettes' mean culpability, here Study 2's, and by payment. UMAP projections are sensitive to their settings and can change across runs and package versions, so these plots are exploratory and suited to supplementary material rather than to primary figures. Because the texts and the model are the ones Study 1 used, the projection does not depend on the study. The Study 1 figure that colors it by each of the six features (fig_umap_by_feature.pdf) therefore applies to Study 2 unchanged and is not redrawn.

Addition. The vignette means of the two studies are compared directly: each of the 64 vignettes contributes its mean culpability in Study 1 and in Study 2. How strongly they agree sets a ceiling on how well any vignette-level result, the RSA included, can replicate, since each vignette mean rests on only about 17 trials in Study 1 and 20 in Study 2.

In [7]:
# ── Vignette-level statistics, one table per outcome ──
def vignette_table(d, outcome="culpability", judgment_col="judgment"):
    t = d.groupby("vignette_id").agg(
        mean_culp=(outcome, "mean"),
        mean_belief=("belief", "mean"),
        n_trials=(outcome, "count"),
        pct_knowledge=(judgment_col, lambda x: (x == "Knowledge").mean()),
        **{c: (c, "first") for c in FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER})
    return t.reindex(VIGNETTE_IDS).reset_index()

vignette_stats_s1 = vignette_table(d1)
vignette_stats = vignette_table(d2)                                   # Study 2, the choice
vignette_stats_probe = vignette_table(d2, "probe_culpability", "probe_judgment")
for t in (vignette_stats_s1, vignette_stats, vignette_stats_probe):
    assert t["n_trials"].notna().all(), "every vignette must have been shown"

# ── Fit UMAP on the 64 vignette embeddings (BGE, the Study 1 settings) ──
reducer = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=10, min_dist=0.1,
                    metric='cosine', random_state=SEED)
umap_coords = reducer.fit_transform(vignette_embeddings_bge)
for t in (vignette_stats_s1, vignette_stats, vignette_stats_probe):
    t["umap_x"], t["umap_y"] = umap_coords[:, 0], umap_coords[:, 1]

print(f"UMAP fitted on {len(umap_coords)} unique vignettes (BGE-large).")
print(f"Trials per vignette: Study 1 {vignette_stats_s1['n_trials'].min()} to {vignette_stats_s1['n_trials'].max()}, "
      f"Study 2 {vignette_stats['n_trials'].min()} to {vignette_stats['n_trials'].max()}")

# ── Addition: vignette means in Study 1 against Study 2 ──
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4.5))
cross_study = []
for ax, col, label, lims in [(axes[0], 'mean_culp', 'mean culpability (1–4)', (1, 4)),
                             (axes[1], 'mean_belief', 'mean belief rating (0–100)', (0, 100))]:
    x, y = vignette_stats_s1[col].values, vignette_stats[col].values
    r, p_r = stats.pearsonr(x, y)
    rho, p_rho = stats.spearmanr(x, y)
    cross_study.append({'Vignette mean': label, 'Pearson r': r, 'p (r)': p_r, 'Spearman rho': rho, 'p (rho)': p_rho})
    ax.scatter(x, y, s=25, color='black', alpha=0.7)
    ax.plot(lims, lims, linestyle=':', color='grey', linewidth=1)
    ax.set_xlim(lims); ax.set_ylim(lims)
    ax.set_xlabel(f'Study 1 {label}')
    ax.set_ylabel(f'Study 2 {label}')
    ax.annotate(f'r = {r:.2f}, ρ = {rho:.2f}', xy=(0.05, 0.95), xycoords='axes fraction', fontsize=9, va='top')
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig('fig_s2_vignette_means_s1_vs_s2.pdf')

5. Random Forest Classification¶

As in Study 1, three random forests predict the four-level judgment. Model A uses only the six binary vignette features; it is the clean test of whether the objective stimulus properties alone predict the category, without the circularity of using a participant's own rating to predict that participant's choice. Model B adds the belief rating as a seventh predictor, and Model C uses the belief rating alone. B and C describe how the judgment relates to the participant's own estimate rather than what causes it, because the rating is itself a response. All three use 10-fold stratified cross-validation with balanced class weights, 500 trees and a minimum of five trials per leaf, and the folds are compared with paired t tests, as in the manuscript's Table A.3.

The same code runs on Study 1. Its results should equal the Study 1 notebook and Table A.3: features only .307 ± .035 (κ = .074), belief rating only .399 ± .035 (κ = .189), features and belief rating .473 ± .029 (κ = .254).

Addition. The three models are also fitted with Study 2's probe-defined category as the outcome.

In [10]:
# ── Random forest settings (Study 1) and cross-validation ──
RF_PARAMS = dict(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=None, min_samples_leaf=5,
    class_weight='balanced', random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1
)

def cv_evaluate(model, X, y):
    # 10-fold stratified CV as in the Study 1 notebook. cross_val_predict refits the model on the same
    # folds that cross_val_score uses, so the per-fold accuracies equal the Study 1 notebook's.
    cv = StratifiedKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=SEED)
    pred = cross_val_predict(model, X, y, cv=cv)
    folds = np.array([accuracy_score(y[test], pred[test]) for _, test in cv.split(X, y)])
    return {"pred": pred, "folds": folds, "acc": folds.mean(), "sd": folds.std(),
            "kappa": cohen_kappa_score(y, pred)}

MODEL_SPECS = {"A": ("Features only (6 predictors)", FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER),
               "B": ("Features + belief rating (7 predictors)", FEATURE_COLS),
               "C": ("Belief rating only (1 predictor)", ["belief"])}

# The three outcomes: Study 1 (the rerun), Study 2, and Study 2's probe-defined category (addition).
OUTCOMES = {"Study 1": (d1, "culpability"),
            "Study 2": (d2, "culpability"),
            "Study 2 probe-defined": (d2, "probe_culpability")}

rf_res = {}
for label, (d, target) in OUTCOMES.items():
    t0 = time.time()
    y_out = d[target].values
    rf_res[label] = {"y": y_out}
    for k, (_, cols) in MODEL_SPECS.items():
        rf_res[label][k] = cv_evaluate(RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS), d[cols].values, y_out)
    print(f"{label}: three models cross-validated in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

                     "Kappa": r["kappa"], "Knowledge recall": np.mean(r["pred"][y_out == 4] == 4),
                     "Majority rate": pd.Series(y_out).value_counts(normalize=True).max()})
    for a, b, name in [("A", "B", "features vs combined"), ("A", "C", "features vs belief only"),
                       ("C", "B", "belief only vs combined")]:
        t, p = stats.ttest_rel(res[a]["folds"], res[b]["folds"])
        tests.append({"Outcome": label, "Comparison": f"{a} vs {b} ({name})",
                      "Accuracy difference": res[b]["acc"] - res[a]["acc"], "t(9)": t, "p": p})
rf_table, rf_tests = pd.DataFrame(rows), pd.DataFrame(tests)

6. SHAP Feature Importance¶

As in Study 1, SHAP values are computed with TreeExplainer (exact for tree models) for both Study 2 forests fitted to all trials: the features-only model, which shows which objective vignette features drive the classification without the belief rating, and the full model, which shows the weight of the participant's own estimate. The figures are the Study 1 set: global bar plots for both models, an overall importance bar, a beeswarm plot for each category and the category-by-feature heatmap.

In [13]:
# ── Fit both RF models on all Study 2 trials for SHAP ──
def shap_3d(sv):
    # TreeExplainer output as an array (trials, features, classes), whatever form the shap version returns.
    if isinstance(sv, list):
        sv = np.array(sv).transpose(1, 2, 0)
    return sv

X_feat = d2[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values
X_full = d2[FEATURE_COLS].values
y = d2["culpability"].values

rf_feat_full = RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS).fit(X_feat, y)
rf_all_full = RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS).fit(X_full, y)

# ── SHAP for features-only model (primary) ──
explainer_feat = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_feat_full)
shap_values_feat = shap_3d(explainer_feat.shap_values(X_feat))
X_display_feat = pd.DataFrame(X_feat, columns=FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER)
print(f"Features-only SHAP shape: {shap_values_feat.shape}")

# ── SHAP for full model (secondary) ──
explainer_full = shap.TreeExplainer(rf_all_full)
shap_values_full = shap_3d(explainer_full.shap_values(X_full))
X_display_full = pd.DataFrame(X_full, columns=FEATURE_LABELS)
print(f"Full model SHAP shape: {shap_values_full.shape}")

# ── Global SHAP bar plots: computed manually for full control ──
# shap.summary_plot manages its own figure internally and ignores pre-created
# axes, so we compute mean |SHAP| per class ourselves and plot with matplotlib.
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))
gray_shades = ['#d9d9d9', '#969696', '#525252', '#000000']

for ax, sv, labels, title in [
    (axes[0], shap_values_feat, FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER, 'A: Features Only (6 predictors)'),
    (axes[1], shap_values_full, FEATURE_LABELS, 'B: Features + Belief Rating (7 predictors)')
]:
    mean_shap = np.mean(np.abs(sv), axis=0)           # (n_features, n_classes)
    bottom = np.zeros(mean_shap.shape[0])
    sorted_idx = np.argsort(mean_shap.mean(axis=1))   # sort by overall importance
    for c in range(mean_shap.shape[1]):
        ax.barh(np.arange(len(sorted_idx)), mean_shap[sorted_idx, c],
                left=bottom[sorted_idx], color=gray_shades[c],
                edgecolor='white', linewidth=0.3, label=JUDGMENT_ORDER[c])
        bottom += mean_shap[:, c]
    ax.set_yticks(np.arange(len(sorted_idx)))
    ax.set_yticklabels([labels[i] for i in sorted_idx])
    ax.set_xlabel('Mean |SHAP value|')
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11)
    ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='lower right')

plt.tight_layout()
save_fig('fig_s2_shap_bar_global.pdf')

Does the Study 1 pattern replicate?¶

In Study 1 the category-specific importances differed: source led for Blamelessness (mean |SHAP| = .115, payment second at .070), payment led for Negligence (.057) and Recklessness (.088), and contents led for Knowledge (.049, ahead of payment at .042), which the manuscript read as participants inferring knowledge from what was in the package. The cell below fits the same features-only forest to each outcome (Study 1, Study 2, and, as an addition, Study 2's probe-defined category) and sets the three importance tables side by side.

The six binary features take at most 64 distinct values, and a trial's SHAP values depend only on its feature values, so the mean over trials is computed from the distinct feature rows weighted by how often each occurs. The result equals the mean over all trials (the cell checks this against the Study 2 values above) and is about twenty times faster, which makes the bootstrap below practical.

In [18]:
# ── Class-specific importance for all three outcomes ──
def class_importance(model, X):
    # Mean |SHAP| for each feature (rows) and category (columns) over the trials in X, computed from the
    # distinct feature rows weighted by their counts. Equal to the mean over all trials.
    rows, counts = np.unique(X, axis=0, return_counts=True)
    sv = np.abs(shap_3d(shap.TreeExplainer(model).shap_values(rows)))
    assert sv.shape[2] == len(JUDGMENT_ORDER), "every category must occur in the data"
    return np.tensordot(counts / counts.sum(), sv, axes=1)

importance = {}
for label, (d, target) in OUTCOMES.items():
    X = d[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values
    m = RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS).fit(X, d[target].values)
    importance[label] = pd.DataFrame(class_importance(m, X), index=FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER, columns=JUDGMENT_ORDER)
assert np.allclose(importance["Study 2"].values, class_importance_s2), "shortcut differs from the mean over trials"

for label, imp in importance.items():
    print(f"── {label}: mean |SHAP| by feature (rows) and category (columns) ──")
    print(imp.round(3).to_string())
    print()

rows = []
for label, imp in importance.items():
    for cls in JUDGMENT_ORDER:
        s = imp[cls].sort_values(ascending=False)
        rows.append({"Outcome": label, "Category": cls, "First": s.index[0], "First |SHAP|": s.iloc[0],
                     "Second": s.index[1], "Second |SHAP|": s.iloc[1],
                     "Contents |SHAP|": imp.loc["Contents (fentanyl)", cls],
                     "Payment |SHAP|": imp.loc["Payment ($1000)", cls]})
top_features = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(top_features.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print()
print("Study 1 manuscript: Blamelessness, Source .115 (Payment .070); Negligence, Payment .057; "
      "Recklessness, Payment .088; Knowledge, Contents .049 (Payment .042).")

long = pd.concat([imp.reset_index(names="Feature").melt(id_vars="Feature", var_name="Category",
                                                           value_name="Mean |SHAP|").assign(Outcome=label)
                  for label, imp in importance.items()])[["Outcome", "Feature", "Category", "Mean |SHAP|"]]
save_table(long, "shap_class_importance.csv")
save_table(top_features, "shap_top_features.csv")

# ── Side-by-side heatmaps with one shared scale ──

Addition: the plain percentages behind the Knowledge importances. A mean |SHAP| value is a size without a direction: it says how much a feature moves the predicted probability of a category, not whether it raises or lowers it. The table below shows the same information without a model and with the direction: the percentage of trials classified as Knowledge at each level of each feature, and the difference in percentage points (level 1 minus level 0). A feature that SHAP ranks first for Knowledge should show the largest difference, and the sign shows which way it works.

Addition: how stable is the ranking? A single forest fitted to one sample gives one ranking, and differences as small as Study 1's .049 against .042 can reverse in a new sample of the same size. The participant bootstrap below draws people with replacement (keeping each person's five trials together), refits the features-only forest to each resample with the Study 1 settings, and recomputes the importance table. The summary gives, for each outcome and category, the percentage of resamples in which each feature ranks first, and for Knowledge the percentage in which contents outranks payment. A ranking that holds in, say, 90% or more of resamples is stable; one near 50% is not distinguishable from a tie. With N_BOOT = 200 this cell takes about ten minutes on two processor cores; lowering N_BOOT in the setup cell shortens it at the cost of coarser percentages.

In [20]:
# ── Participant bootstrap of the class-specific importance ──
def bootstrap_importance(d, target, n_boot=N_BOOT, seed=SEED):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    people = list(d.groupby("pid").indices.values())        # row positions of each person's five trials
    X_all, y_all = d[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values, d[target].values
    out = np.empty((n_boot, len(FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER), len(JUDGMENT_ORDER)))
    for b in range(n_boot):
        idx = np.concatenate([people[i] for i in rng.integers(0, len(people), len(people))])
        m = RandomForestClassifier(**dict(RF_PARAMS, random_state=SEED + 1 + b)).fit(X_all[idx], y_all[idx])
        out[b] = class_importance(m, X_all[idx])
    return out

boot = {}
for label, (d, target) in OUTCOMES.items():
    t0 = time.time()
    boot[label] = bootstrap_importance(d, target)
    print(f"{label}: {N_BOOT} resamples in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

# ── How often each feature ranks first, by outcome and category ──
rows = []
for label, B in boot.items():
    first = B.argmax(axis=1)                                  # (n_boot, n_classes): index of the top feature
    for c, cls in enumerate(JUDGMENT_ORDER):
        rows.append({"Outcome": label, "Category": cls,
                     **{name: 100 * np.mean(first[:, c] == f) for f, name in enumerate(FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER)}})
rank_first = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print()
print("Percentage of resamples in which each feature ranks first:")
print(rank_first.round(0).to_string(index=False))

# ── Knowledge: contents against payment ──
K = JUDGMENT_ORDER.index("Knowledge")
ci_, pi_ = FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER.index("Contents (fentanyl)"), FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER.index("Payment ($1000)")
rows = []
for label, B in boot.items():
    kb = B[:, :, K]
    diff = kb[:, ci_] - kb[:, pi_]
    lo, hi = np.percentile(diff, [2.5, 97.5])
    rows.append({"Outcome": label,
                 "Contents |SHAP|": importance[label].iloc[ci_, K],
                 "Payment |SHAP|": importance[label].iloc[pi_, K],
                 "Contents minus payment": importance[label].iloc[ci_, K] - importance[label].iloc[pi_, K],
                 "95% bootstrap interval": f"[{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]",
                 "Contents > payment (% of resamples)": 100 * np.mean(diff > 0)})
knowledge_boot = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print()
print("Knowledge: contents against payment")
print(knowledge_boot.round(3).to_string(index=False))

boot_long = pd.DataFrame([{"Outcome": label, "Resample": b + 1, "Feature": FEATURE_LABELS_NO_SLIDER[f],
                           "Category": JUDGMENT_ORDER[c], "Mean |SHAP|": B[b, f, c]}
                          for label, B in boot.items() for b in range(B.shape[0])
                          for f in range(B.shape[1]) for c in range(B.shape[2])])
save_table(boot_long, "shap_bootstrap.csv")
save_table(rank_first, "shap_bootstrap_rank_first.csv")
save_table(knowledge_boot, "shap_bootstrap_knowledge.csv")

The figure shows, for the Knowledge category, each feature's importance in all trials (bars) and the range of the middle 95% of its bootstrap values (lines). The ranges sit somewhat to the right of the bars: a resample repeats some people, which lets the forest fit their answers more closely and inflates every mean |SHAP| value. The inflation applies to all six features within a resample, so the rankings and the contents-against-payment percentages above, which compare features within each resample, are the quantities to read.

7. SHAP Dependence and Interaction Effects¶

Dependence plots show how the SHAP value for a feature varies with the feature's value; for binary features this gives two clusters of points, and color marks the feature SHAP selects as the strongest interaction. As in Study 1, the plots are for the Recklessness class and show the two features with the highest overall importance in the features-only model (in Study 1, payment and source; here they are chosen from the Study 2 values). The interaction heatmap uses the first 200 trials, as in Study 1.

8. Representational Similarity Analysis (RSA)¶

Do vignettes that are semantically closer in embedding space elicit more similar culpability judgments? As in Study 1, we compute the pairwise cosine distances between the 64 vignette embeddings and correlate them (Spearman) with the pairwise differences in mean culpability, three ways: BGE-large on the full text (primary), MiniLM on the full text (a check), and BGE-large on the clauses that vary between conditions only, which removes the dilution from the shared template text. In Study 1 the three correlations were ρ = .077 (p = .0006), .019 (p = .395) and .129 (p < .0001), across 2,016 vignette pairs.

Addition: a permutation p value. The p values from scipy.stats.spearmanr treat the 2,016 pairs as independent observations, but each vignette enters 63 pairs, so they overstate the evidence. The standard remedy in RSA (a Mantel test) shuffles the 64 vignette means across vignettes, recomputes the correlation each time, and reports the share of shuffles with a correlation at least as large in absolute value. Both p values are reported; the pair-based one only for comparison with Study 1. The analysis runs on Study 1 (the rerun), on Study 2 and, as a further addition, on Study 2's probe-defined category.

In [24]:
# ── Helper functions for RSA ──
def cosine_vector(embedding_dict):
    # Cosine distances for the 2,016 vignette pairs, in the order of np.triu_indices(64, k=1).
    emb_matrix = np.array([embedding_dict[k] for k in VIGNETTE_IDS])
    return pdist(emb_matrix, metric='cosine')

def compute_rsa(cos_vec, means, n_perm=N_PERM, seed=SEED):
    # Spearman correlation between embedding distances and judgment distances, with the pair-based
    # p value (as in Study 1) and a permutation p value that shuffles the vignette means.
    means = np.asarray(means, dtype=float)
    culp_vec = pdist(means.reshape(-1, 1), metric='cityblock')
    rho, p_pairs = stats.spearmanr(cos_vec, culp_vec)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    rank_cos = stats.rankdata(cos_vec)
    null = np.array([np.corrcoef(rank_cos, stats.rankdata(pdist(rng.permutation(means).reshape(-1, 1),
                                                                    metric='cityblock')))[0, 1]
                     for _ in range(n_perm)])
    p_perm = (1 + np.sum(np.abs(null) >= abs(rho))) / (1 + n_perm)
    return {"rho": rho, "p_pairs": p_pairs, "p_perm": p_perm, "culp_vec": culp_vec}

# ── Clause-level texts (the Study 1 wording) ──
def extract_varying_clauses(row):
    # Build a string of just the feature-specific text for a vignette.
    parts = []
    parts.append("Mexico" if row['location_bin'] == 1 else "Canada")
    parts.append("a biker" if row['source_bin'] == 1 else "his uncle")
    parts.append("a large duffel bag" if row['package_bin'] == 1 else "a gift-wrapped package")
    parts.append("His uncle tells him it is just coffee" if row['inquiry_bin'] == 1
                 else "He asks what is inside and his uncle says it is just coffee")
    parts.append("for one thousand dollars" if row['payment_bin'] == 1
                 else "without asking for payment")
    parts.append("fentanyl, a potent narcotic drug" if row['contents_bin'] == 1
                 else "drugs to treat a rare disease not yet approved in the US")
    return " | ".join(parts)

clause_texts = vignette_stats.apply(extract_varying_clauses, axis=1).tolist()
clause_embeddings = st_model_bge.encode(clause_texts, normalize_embeddings=True)
key_to_clause_emb = dict(zip(VIGNETTE_IDS, clause_embeddings))

EMBEDDINGS = {"BGE-large (full text)": cosine_vector(key_to_embedding_bge),
              "MiniLM (full text)": cosine_vector(key_to_embedding_mini),
              "BGE-large (clauses only)": cosine_vector(key_to_clause_emb)}
MEANS = {"Study 1": vignette_stats_s1["mean_culp"].values,
         "Study 2": vignette_stats["mean_culp"].values,
         "Study 2 probe-defined": vignette_stats_probe["mean_culp"].values}

rsa_results, rows = {}, []
for outcome, means in MEANS.items():
    print("═" * 60)
    print(f"RSA: {outcome}")
    print("═" * 60)
    for emb_label, cos_vec in EMBEDDINGS.items():
        res = compute_rsa(cos_vec, means)
        rsa_results[(outcome, emb_label)] = res
        print(f"  {emb_label}: ρ = {res['rho']:.3f}, p = {res['p_pairs']:.4f} (pairs), "
              f"p = {res['p_perm']:.4f} (permutation) (N pairs = {len(cos_vec)})")
        rows.append({"Outcome": outcome, "Embedding": emb_label, "rho": res["rho"],
                     "p (pairs, as in Study 1)": res["p_pairs"], "p (permutation)": res["p_perm"],
                     "Pairs": len(cos_vec), "Permutations": N_PERM})
    print()
rsa_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Study 1 notebook: BGE full text ρ = 0.077, p = 0.0006; MiniLM ρ = 0.019, p = 0.3949; "
      "BGE clauses ρ = 0.129, p < 0.0001 (pair-based p values).")
save_table(rsa_table, "rsa.csv")

# ── RSA scatter plots: all three analyses (Study 2) ──
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.5))
for ax, (emb_label, cos_vec), title in zip(axes, EMBEDDINGS.items(),
                                           ['BGE-large (full text)', 'MiniLM (full text)', 'BGE-large (clauses only)']):
    res = rsa_results[("Study 2", emb_label)]
    culp_vec = res["culp_vec"]
    ax.scatter(cos_vec, culp_vec, alpha=0.15, s=10, color='black')
    z = np.polyfit(cos_vec, culp_vec, 1)
    x_line = np.linspace(cos_vec.min(), cos_vec.max(), 100)
    ax.plot(x_line, np.poly1d(z)(x_line), color='black', linewidth=1.5, linestyle='--')
    ax.set_xlabel('Cosine Distance')
    ax.set_ylabel('|Δ Mean Culpability|')
    ax.annotate(f"ρ = {res['rho']:.3f}, permutation p = {res['p_perm']:.4f}",
                xy=(0.05, 0.95), xycoords='axes fraction', fontsize=9, va='top')
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
plt.tight_layout()

The single-feature embedding distances below depend only on the vignette texts and the embedding models, so they are the same for both studies; they are recomputed as a check that the embeddings reproduce Study 1's. In Study 1 they were, for BGE-large: location .0443, contents .0380, source .0127, payment .0117, package .0079 and inquiry .0042. The Study 1 figure (fig_embedding_feature_distances.pdf) applies to Study 2 unchanged.

In [26]:
# ── Feature-specific embedding distances (the same for both studies) ──
# For each binary feature, the mean cosine distance between vignettes that differ only on that feature.
cos_mat_bge = squareform(EMBEDDINGS["BGE-large (full text)"])
cos_mat_mini = squareform(EMBEDDINGS["MiniLM (full text)"])
B_ = vignette_stats[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values
rows = []
for f, label in enumerate(['Source', 'Package', 'Inquiry', 'Payment', 'Location', 'Contents']):
    others = [j for j in range(6) if j != f]
    pairs = [(i, j) for i in range(64) for j in range(i + 1, 64)
             if B_[i, f] != B_[j, f] and (B_[i, others] == B_[j, others]).all()]
    rows.append({'Feature': label,
                 'BGE dist': np.mean([cos_mat_bge[i, j] for i, j in pairs]),
                 'MiniLM dist': np.mean([cos_mat_mini[i, j] for i, j in pairs]),
                 'N pairs': len(pairs)})
fd_df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
for _, r in fd_df.iterrows():
    print(f"  {r['Feature']}: BGE={r['BGE dist']:.4f}, MiniLM={r['MiniLM dist']:.4f} ({r['N pairs']} pairs)")
save_table(fd_df, "embedding_feature_distances.csv")

9. Free-Text Justification Analysis¶

Each participant wrote a brief justification after each choice. As in Study 1, justifications longer than five characters are embedded with BGE-large and projected with UMAP, colored by the choice. In Study 2 each justification was written after the choice and the belief rating and before the three probe questions.

Addition. The Study 2 projection is also colored by the probe-defined category. The Study 1 justifications are embedded too, for the Study 1 rerun of the text classifier in Section 10.

In [27]:
# ── Justification texts (more than five characters, as in Study 1) ──
def with_text(d):
    text = d["justification"].fillna("").astype(str).str.strip()
    return d.assign(justification_clean=text)[text.str.len() > 5].copy()

d1_just, d_just = with_text(d1), with_text(d2)
print(f"Trials with justification text (>5 chars): Study 1 {len(d1_just)} / {len(d1)}; Study 2 {len(d_just)} / {len(d2)}")

# ── Embed justification texts with BGE (primary model) ──
just_texts = d_just["justification_clean"].tolist()
t0 = time.time()
just_embeddings = st_model_bge.encode(just_texts, batch_size=32, normalize_embeddings=True)
just_embeddings_s1 = st_model_bge.encode(d1_just["justification_clean"].tolist(), batch_size=32,
                                         normalize_embeddings=True)
print(f"Embedded {len(just_texts)} Study 2 and {len(d1_just)} Study 1 justifications with BGE-large "
      f"in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

# ── UMAP on Study 2 justifications ──
reducer_just = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1,
                         metric='cosine', random_state=SEED)
just_umap = reducer_just.fit_transform(just_embeddings)
d_just['just_umap_x'] = just_umap[:, 0]
d_just['just_umap_y'] = just_umap[:, 1]

gray_palette = {'Blamelessness': '#d9d9d9', 'Negligence': '#969696',
                'Recklessness': '#525252', 'Knowledge': '#000000'}

def justification_map(column, legend_title, name):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6))
    for judgment in JUDGMENT_ORDER:
        subset = d_just[d_just[column] == judgment]
        ax.scatter(subset['just_umap_x'], subset['just_umap_y'],
                   c=gray_palette[judgment], label=judgment,
                   s=20, alpha=0.6, edgecolors='black', linewidth=0.2)
    ax.set_xlabel('UMAP 1')
    ax.set_ylabel('UMAP 2')
    ax.legend(loc='best', title=legend_title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    save_fig(name)

10. BERTopic & Text-to-Judgment Classification¶

BERTopic finds recurring themes in the justifications through sentence embeddings, UMAP, HDBSCAN clustering and class-based TF-IDF, and each justification is assigned to a topic (or to the outlier group, topic −1). As in Study 1, the model is fitted twice, once with the BGE embeddings and once with MiniLM, whose smaller embedding space gives the density-based clustering more structure to work with and in Study 1 yielded far more topics (23, against 3 with BGE). For each topic the notebook prints its size, its eight top keywords and its mix of categories. It does not print the example justifications BERTopic stores for each topic, so that no individual justification appears in the output; the topic tables are saved without them.

The text classifier asks whether a simple model can predict the choice from the justification embedding alone: a logistic regression on the BGE embeddings, with 10-fold cross-validation, as in Study 1 (accuracy .519 ± .037, κ = .237).

Additions. The MiniLM topics are also crossed with the probe-defined category and, if data/processed/justification_codes.csv is in the folder, with the registered justification codes, which shows what each topic contains in the codebook's terms. The classifier is also run on Study 1 (the rerun) and with the probe-defined category as the outcome, and once more with balanced class weights, so that its recall of Knowledge does not depend on how common Knowledge is.

In [28]:
# ── BERTopic on justification texts (BGE) ──
def describe_topics(model, topic_col, judgment_col="judgment"):
    # One row per topic: size, top keywords and category mix. No example texts.
    rows = []
    for topic_id in sorted(t for t in model.get_topics() if t != -1):
        sub = d_just[d_just[topic_col] == topic_id]
        mix = sub[judgment_col].value_counts(normalize=True).reindex(JUDGMENT_ORDER, fill_value=0) * 100
        rows.append({"Topic": topic_id, "n": len(sub),
                     "Keywords": ", ".join(w for w, _ in model.get_topic(topic_id)[:8]),
                     "Dominant": mix.idxmax(), "Dominant %": mix.max(),
                     **{f"{c} %": mix[c] for c in JUDGMENT_ORDER}})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

def print_topics(table, label):
    print("═" * 60)
    print(f"{label} Topic Descriptions (representative keywords)")
    print("═" * 60)
    for _, r in table.iterrows():
        print(f"  Topic {r['Topic']:2d} (n={r['n']:3d}, dominant={r['Dominant']} {r['Dominant %']:.0f}%): {r['Keywords']}")

def topic_crosstab(topic_col, judgment_col, legend_title, name):
    crosstab = pd.crosstab(d_just[topic_col], d_just[judgment_col], normalize='index')
    crosstab = crosstab.reindex(columns=JUDGMENT_ORDER, fill_value=0) * 100
    crosstab = crosstab.drop(index=-1, errors='ignore')
    if len(crosstab) > 1:
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, max(4, len(crosstab) * 0.4)))
        crosstab.plot(kind='barh', stacked=True, ax=ax,
                      color=['#d9d9d9', '#969696', '#525252', '#000000'],
                      edgecolor='black', linewidth=0.3)
        ax.set_xlabel('% of Justifications in Topic')
        ax.set_ylabel('Topic')
        ax.legend(title=legend_title, bbox_to_anchor=(1.05, 1), loc='upper left')
        plt.tight_layout()
        save_fig(name)
    else:
        print("Only one topic found; no crosstab to plot.")

if BERTOPIC_AVAILABLE:
    topic_model = BERTopic(
        embedding_model=st_model_bge,
        umap_model=umap.UMAP(n_components=5, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.0,
                             metric='cosine', random_state=SEED),
        nr_topics='auto',
        verbose=False
    )
    topics, probs = topic_model.fit_transform(just_texts, just_embeddings)
    d_just['topic'] = topics
    topics_bge = describe_topics(topic_model, 'topic')
    print(f"Number of topics discovered: {len(topics_bge)} (outliers, topic -1: {(d_just['topic'] == -1).sum()})")
    print()
    print_topics(topics_bge, "BGE")
    save_table(topics_bge, "topics_bge.csv")
    topic_crosstab('topic', 'judgment', 'Judgment', 'fig_s2_bertopic_judgment.pdf')
else:
    print("BERTopic not available. Install with: pip install bertopic")

BERTopic with MiniLM (robustness comparison)¶

As in Study 1, the topic model is refitted with MiniLM embeddings. BGE-large's 1024-dimensional embeddings concentrate short justifications in a dense region of the space and so give HDBSCAN few clusters; the smaller MiniLM space usually separates more themes. This reflects how embedding geometry interacts with density-based clustering, not a weakness of BGE for the RSA or the classifier.

In [29]:

    topic_model_mini = BERTopic(
        embedding_model=st_model_mini,
        umap_model=umap.UMAP(n_components=5, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.0,

        nr_topics='auto',

# ── Text-to-judgment classification ──
# Can the justification embedding alone predict the mental state judgment?
def text_classifier(embeddings, y_text):
    lr = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, C=1.0, random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
    return cv_evaluate(lr, embeddings, y_text)

TEXT_OUTCOMES = {"Study 1": (just_embeddings_s1, d1_just["culpability"].values),
                 "Study 2": (just_embeddings, d_just["culpability"].values),
                 "Study 2 probe-defined": (just_embeddings, d_just["probe_culpability"].values)}
text_res = {label: text_classifier(emb, y_text) for label, (emb, y_text) in TEXT_OUTCOMES.items()}

y_text = d_just["culpability"].values
r = text_res["Study 2"]
print("Text-only classification (BGE embeddings, 10-fold CV), Study 2:")
print(f"  Accuracy: {r['acc']:.3f} ± {r['sd']:.3f}")
print(f"  Cohen's κ: {r['kappa']:.3f}")
print(f"  Chance level: {1/4:.3f} (uniform) or "
      f"{pd.Series(y_text).value_counts(normalize=True).max():.3f} (majority class)")
print()
print(classification_report(y_text, r["pred"], target_names=JUDGMENT_ORDER))

rows = []
for label, res in text_res.items():
    y_out = TEXT_OUTCOMES[label][1]
    rows.append({"Outcome": label, "Justifications": len(y_out), "Accuracy": res["acc"], "SD": res["sd"],
                 "Kappa": res["kappa"], "Majority rate": pd.Series(y_out).value_counts(normalize=True).max(),
                 "Knowledge recall": np.mean(res["pred"][y_out == 4] == 4)})
text_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(text_table.round(3).to_string(index=False))
print("Study 1 notebook: accuracy 0.519 ± 0.037, κ = 0.237, Knowledge recall 0.02.")
save_table(text_table, "text_classification.csv")

# ── Addition: the same classifier with balanced class weights ──
# Without class weights a logistic regression rarely predicts a small category, so the recall of
# Knowledge depends on how common Knowledge is (about 10% of choices but 25% of probe-defined
# categories in Study 2). Balanced weights put the categories on an equal footing.
rows = []
for label, (emb, y_out) in TEXT_OUTCOMES.items():
    lr_bal = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, C=1.0, class_weight='balanced', random_state=SEED, n_jobs=-1)
    res = cv_evaluate(lr_bal, emb, y_out)
    recall = {f"{c} recall": np.mean(res["pred"][y_out == k + 1] == k + 1) for k, c in enumerate(JUDGMENT_ORDER)}
    rows.append({"Outcome": label, "Accuracy": res["acc"], "SD": res["sd"], "Kappa": res["kappa"], **recall})
text_balanced = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print()
print("Balanced class weights:")
print(text_balanced.round(3).to_string(index=False))
save_table(text_balanced, "text_classification_balanced.csv")

# ── Confusion matrix (Study 2) ──
cm_text = confusion_matrix(y_text, r["pred"])
cm_text_pct = cm_text.astype(float) / cm_text.sum(axis=1, keepdims=True) * 100
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
sns.heatmap(cm_text_pct, annot=True, fmt='.1f', cmap='Greys',
            xticklabels=JUDGMENT_ORDER, yticklabels=JUDGMENT_ORDER,
            cbar_kws={'label': '% of True Class'}, linewidths=0.5,
            linecolor='black', ax=ax)
ax.set_xlabel('Predicted')
ax.set_ylabel('Actual')
plt.tight_layout()
save_fig('fig_s2_text_classification_cm.pdf')

11. Combined Feature + Text Model¶

As in Study 1, we test whether adding the justification embedding to the feature-based model improves classification, which tells us whether participants' written reasoning carries information about their choice beyond what the vignette features and the belief rating capture. All models are fitted to the trials with a justification, with the same folds. In Study 1 the combined model (features and text, .531 ± .042) outperformed both the features alone (.315 ± .051; t = 13.99, p < .001) and the features with the belief rating (.470 ± .062; t = 3.83, p = .004). The comparison runs on Study 2 and on Study 1 (the rerun).

Embeddings computed on a CPU and on a GPU differ in their last digits. The logistic regression above is not affected, but a forest that splits on the 1,024 embedding dimensions can be, so without a GPU the combined model's Study 1 numbers can differ slightly from the published ones (a CPU test run gave .531 ± .041, t = 14.46 and t = 3.69).

In [32]:
# ── Combined: features + text embedding ──
def combined_models(dj, embeddings, text_result):
    y_c = dj["culpability"].values
    feat = cv_evaluate(RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS), dj[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values, y_c)
    full = cv_evaluate(RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS), dj[FEATURE_COLS].values, y_c)
    comb = cv_evaluate(RandomForestClassifier(**RF_PARAMS),
                       np.hstack([dj[FEATURE_COLS_NO_SLIDER].values, embeddings]), y_c)
    return {"Features only (6 binary)": feat, "Features + belief rating (7)": full,
            "Text embedding only (BGE)": text_result, "Features + text (6 + BGE)": comb}

combined, rows = {}, []
for label, dj, emb in [("Study 2", d_just, just_embeddings), ("Study 1", d1_just, just_embeddings_s1)]:
    t0 = time.time()
    res = combined_models(dj, emb, text_res[label])
    combined[label] = res
    print("═" * 60)
    print(f"Model Comparison (10-fold CV accuracy, justification subset), {label}")
    print("═" * 60)
    for name, r in res.items():
        print(f"  {name:<28} {r['acc']:.3f} ± {r['sd']:.3f}")
        rows.append({"Study": label, "Model": name, "Accuracy": r["acc"], "SD": r["sd"], "Kappa": r["kappa"]})
    comb = res["Features + text (6 + BGE)"]["folds"]
    t1, p1 = stats.ttest_rel(comb, res["Features only (6 binary)"]["folds"])
    t2, p2 = stats.ttest_rel(comb, res["Features + belief rating (7)"]["folds"])
    print()
    print(f"  Combined vs features-only:      t = {t1:.2f}, p = {p1:.4f}")
    print(f"  Combined vs features + belief:  t = {t2:.2f}, p = {p2:.4f}")
    print(f"  ({time.time() - t0:.0f} s)")
    print()
    rows.append({"Study": label, "Model": "t: combined vs features only", "Accuracy": t1, "SD": p1, "Kappa": np.nan})
    rows.append({"Study": label, "Model": "t: combined vs features + belief", "Accuracy": t2, "SD": p2, "Kappa": np.nan})
combined_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print("Study 1 notebook: features .315 ± .051, features + slider .470 ± .062, text .519 ± .037, "
      "features + text .531 ± .042; t = 13.99 (p < .0001) and t = 3.83 (p = .0040).")
print("In the saved table, the rows starting with t hold the t statistic under Accuracy and its p value under SD.")
save_table(combined_table, "combined_models.csv")

12. Replication Summary¶

Addition. The table sets each published Study 1 number (from the Study 1 notebook and the submitted manuscript) beside the same quantity recomputed here from the Study 1 data and its Study 2 counterparts. The rerun column should match the published column; the Study 2 columns are the replication. The table is saved as output/nlp/replication_summary.csv for the combined report.

In [33]:
# ── Replication summary ──
def apa(x, d=3):
    # A number in APA style: no leading zero for values that cannot exceed 1.
    s = f"{x:.{d}f}"
    return s.replace("0.", ".", 1) if abs(x) < 1 else s

def p_eq(p):
    return "p < .0001" if p < 0.0001 else f"p = {apa(p, 4)}"

def acc(r):
    return f"{apa(r['acc'])} ± {apa(r['sd'])} (κ = {apa(r['kappa'])})"

def ttest_text(res, a, b):
    t, p = stats.ttest_rel(res[a]["folds"], res[b]["folds"])
    return f"t(9) = {t:.2f}, {p_eq(p)}"

def top_text(label, cls):
    s = importance[label][cls].sort_values(ascending=False)
    return f"{s.index[0].split(' (')[0]} {apa(s.iloc[0])} ({s.index[1].split(' (')[0]} {apa(s.iloc[1])})"

def knowledge_text(label):
    r = knowledge_boot.set_index("Outcome").loc[label]
    return (f"{apa(r['Contents |SHAP|'])} vs {apa(r['Payment |SHAP|'])}; contents ahead in "
            f"{r['Contents > payment (% of resamples)']:.0f}% of resamples")

def rate_text(label, feature):
    r = knowledge_rates.set_index(["Outcome", "Feature"]).loc[(label, feature)]
    return (f"{r['Knowledge % (level 1)']:.1f}% vs {r['Knowledge % (level 0)']:.1f}% "
            f"({r['Difference (points)']:+.1f} points)")

def rsa_text(outcome, emb):
    r = rsa_results[(outcome, emb)]
    return f"ρ = {apa(r['rho'])} (pairs {p_eq(r['p_pairs'])}; permutation {p_eq(r['p_perm'])})"

def balanced_text(label):
    r = text_balanced.set_index("Outcome").loc[label]
    return f"{apa(r['Accuracy'])} (κ = {apa(r['Kappa'])}); Knowledge recall {apa(r['Knowledge recall'], 2)}"

def combined_text(label, other):
    res = combined[label]
    t, p = stats.ttest_rel(res["Features + text (6 + BGE)"]["folds"], res[other]["folds"])
    return f"{apa(res['Features + text (6 + BGE)']['acc'])} vs {apa(res[other]['acc'])}; t = {t:.2f}, {p_eq(p)}"

O = ["Study 1", "Study 2", "Study 2 probe-defined"]
summary = [
    ("RF, features only", ".307 ± .035 (κ = .074)", *[acc(rf_res[o]["A"]) for o in O]),
    ("RF, belief rating only", ".399 ± .035 (κ = .189)", *[acc(rf_res[o]["C"]) for o in O]),
    ("RF, features + belief rating", ".473 ± .029 (κ = .254)", *[acc(rf_res[o]["B"]) for o in O]),
    ("RF, features vs features + belief", "t(9) = -11.15, p < .0001", *[ttest_text(rf_res[o], "A", "B") for o in O]),
    ("SHAP first (second), Blamelessness", "Source .115 (Payment .070)", *[top_text(o, "Blamelessness") for o in O]),
    ("SHAP first (second), Negligence", "Payment .057", *[top_text(o, "Negligence") for o in O]),
    ("SHAP first (second), Recklessness", "Payment .088", *[top_text(o, "Recklessness") for o in O]),
    ("SHAP first (second), Knowledge", "Contents .049 (Payment .042)", *[top_text(o, "Knowledge") for o in O]),
    ("Knowledge: contents vs payment |SHAP|", ".049 vs .042", *[knowledge_text(o) for o in O]),
    ("Knowledge %, fentanyl vs rare-disease drugs", "not reported", *[rate_text(o, "Contents (fentanyl)") for o in O]),
    ("Knowledge %, $1,000 vs no payment", "not reported", *[rate_text(o, "Payment ($1000)") for o in O]),
    ("RSA, BGE-large full text", "ρ = .077 (pairs p = .0006)", *[rsa_text(o, "BGE-large (full text)") for o in O]),
    ("RSA, MiniLM full text", "ρ = .019 (pairs p = .3949)", *[rsa_text(o, "MiniLM (full text)") for o in O]),
    ("RSA, BGE-large clauses only", "ρ = .129 (pairs p < .0001)", *[rsa_text(o, "BGE-large (clauses only)") for o in O]),
    ("Text classifier (BGE + logistic regression)", ".519 ± .037 (κ = .237)", *[acc(text_res[o]) for o in O]),
    ("Text classifier, balanced class weights", "not run", *[balanced_text(o) for o in O]),

     combined_text("Study 1", "Features only (6 binary)"), combined_text("Study 2", "Features only (6 binary)"), "not run"),

HTML copy of this notebook¶

Save the notebook first (in Colab, File, then Save), then run the cell below. It writes output/nlp/05_nlp_study2.html, a copy of the notebook with all its outputs, after removing the widget data that otherwise breaks the conversion (the same cleaning the Study 1 notebook used). If the saved notebook does not yet contain the outputs of the replication summary, the cell says so and writes nothing.

In [36]:
# ── Save an HTML copy of the notebook with its outputs ──
import nbformat
NOTEBOOK = "05_nlp_study2.ipynb"
if not os.path.exists(NOTEBOOK):
    print(f"{NOTEBOOK} is not in {ROOT}; open the notebook from the study2_analysis folder to make the HTML copy.")
else:
    nb = nbformat.read(NOTEBOOK, as_version=4)
    key = "save_table(" + "replication,"      # written in two parts so that this cell does not match itself
    done = any(c.cell_type == "code" and key in c.source and c.get("outputs") for c in nb.cells)
    if not done:
        print("The saved notebook has no outputs for the replication summary yet. Save the notebook "
              "(File, then Save) and run this cell again.")
    else:
        nb.metadata.pop("widgets", None)
        for cell in nb.cells:
            if "outputs" in cell:
                kept = []
                for output in cell["outputs"]:
                    if "data" in output:
                        output["data"].pop("application/vnd.jupyter.widget-view+json", None)
                        if not output["data"]:
                            continue
                    kept.append(output)
                cell["outputs"] = kept
        clean = os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "05_nlp_study2_for_html.ipynb")
        nbformat.write(nb, clean)
        subprocess.run([sys.executable, "-m", "nbconvert", "--to", "html", "--output", "05_nlp_study2",
                        "--output-dir", OUT_DIR, clean], check=True)
        os.remove(clean)
        print("Saved:", os.path.join(OUT_DIR, "05_nlp_study2.html"))
